title: What Metadata Should You Attach to Customer Feedback Before You Analyze It?
summary: Attach customer ID, date and channel first, then segment, value, product, journey stage and score. Here's what each field lets you answer.
body_markdown:
Attach eight fields to every piece of customer feedback before you analyze it: a customer or account ID, the date, the channel, the product, the customer segment, the journey stage, any score the customer gave, and a measure of customer value. These fields are what make a survey comment, a support ticket and an app review comparable. Without them, you can say what customers talk about. You can't say who said it, where, or how much it matters.


The order matters too. Customer ID, date and channel come first, because you can't add them back later. Segment, product, journey stage, score and value come next. Some of those can be joined on afterward, but only if the customer ID is there.


Thematic builds its analysis filters from whatever columns you supply with the feedback. So every field you attach becomes a way to slice themes later, and every field you skip is a question you can't ask.


## The 5-step process


1. **Capture the three fields you can't recover later:** customer or account ID, date, and channel.
2. **Add the fields that explain who is speaking:** segment and customer value.
3. **Add the fields that explain what they are talking about:** product and journey stage.
4. **Keep the score next to the comment,** in its original scale.
5. **Write down what each field means,** and check what is missing before you analyze.


## Which metadata fields matter most?


Each field unlocks a set of questions. Each missing field closes them off.


Field Questions it lets you answer What you lose without it


Customer or account ID Who said this? What else did they say, on other channels? Joining to customer relationship management (CRM) data, deduplication, and any later enrichment


Date Is this theme growing? Did the release fix it? Trends, before-and-after comparisons


Channel Do support tickets and surveys tell the same story? Separating channel bias from real change


Segment Do enterprise and small business customers want different things? Prioritizing by audience


Customer value How much revenue sits behind this theme? Sizing problems in money terms


Product Which product is the complaint about? Routing issues to the right team


Journey stage Where in the experience does friction happen? Locating the moment to fix


Score Which themes drive detractors? Linking themes to[net promoter score (NPS)](https://getthematic.com/insights/ultimate-guide-to-net-promoter-score) , customer satisfaction (CSAT) or ratings


## Step 1: Capture the fields you can't recover later


These three are almost impossible to rebuild once feedback leaves its source system.


**Customer or account ID** is the most important field on the list. It's the key that lets you join feedback to everything else you know about the customer. Pass it into the survey link at send time, and keep the ticket's requester ID when exporting support data. For business-to-business (B2B) programs, carry the account ID as well as the person, since decisions are made at account level. Data teams will recognize this as the key behind a[master data management](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/master-data-management) "golden record."


**Date** should be the date the customer gave the feedback, not the date you imported it. Store it in one consistent format across sources, such as[ISO 8601](https://www.iso.org/iso-8601-date-and-time-format.html) (YYYY-MM-DD). A batch import stamped with today's date makes every trend chart wrong.


**Channel** records where the feedback came from: survey, support ticket, chat, app review, call transcript. Channels attract different customers in different moods. A theme that only appears in support tickets may be a support problem, not a product one.


Don't assume the source system will keep these three fields. Capture them on the way in.


## Step 2: Add the fields that explain who is speaking


**Segment** is how your business already divides customers: plan or tier, region, industry, company size, tenure. Use the segments your teams already report on. A segment nobody acts on adds noise to every filter list.


**Customer value** is annual revenue, contract value or lifetime value. It's the field that turns "many people mention billing" into "the accounts mentioning billing hold a large share of revenue." Take the value as it stood when the customer responded, not as it is today. Otherwise churned customers show up as worthless and the pattern you need disappears.


Both usually live in the CRM. With the customer ID from Step 1, you can join them on later. The guide on[joining feedback to revenue and CRM data](https://getthematic.com/insights/join-feedback-revenue-crm-data) covers the join keys and match-rate checks.


## Step 3: Add the fields that explain what they are talking about


**Product** names the product, plan feature or service line the feedback refers to. Use one controlled list across channels. "iOS app," "iPhone app" and "mobile" should map to one value before analysis, not after.


**Journey stage** places the feedback in the customer's experience: onboarding, first use, renewal, cancellation.[Nielsen Norman Group](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/customer-journey-mapping/) describes journey maps as organized around "chunkable phases of the journey," and those phases make a good starting list. Many surveys already imply the stage (a post-onboarding survey is about onboarding). Tag it explicitly so it survives when the data is merged with other channels.


The mistake to avoid here is guessing. If you don't know the journey stage of an app review, leave it blank rather than inventing one. A blank value is honest. A wrong one quietly skews every comparison.


## Step 4: Keep the score next to the comment


If the customer gave a rating, NPS, CSAT or effort score with their comment, keep it on the same row, in its original scale. A 1 to 5 star rating and a 0 to 10 NPS response aren't the same measure, so record which scale each score uses.


The score is what[links themes to outcomes](https://getthematic.com/insights/link-feedback-themes-nps-csat-drivers) . With it, you can see which themes are most common among detractors, or which ones pull a CSAT average down. Without it, you have a list of topics and no sense of which ones hurt.


In Thematic, score columns can be filtered by individual value or by buckets, such as Detractor 0 to 6, Passive 7 to 8 and Promoter 9 to 10.


## Step 5: Write down what each field means, then check the gaps


A field is only comparable across channels if it means the same thing in each one. Write a short definition for each field: its name, its allowed values, its source system and who owns it. This is the same discipline that underpins a[single source of truth](https://getthematic.com/insights/single-source-of-truth-customer-feedback) for customer feedback.


Then check coverage before you analyze. For each field, count how many rows are missing it, broken out by channel. If nearly every survey row has a customer ID but almost no app reviews do, any account-level finding speaks for survey respondents only. Say so in the readout.


## How does metadata change what you can ask in Thematic?


Thematic turns the columns you supply into filters across its analysis tools and dashboards. A few behaviors make the fields above especially useful:


- **Any column can become a filter.** Region, tier, product or journey stage all appear in the filter bar once they are in the data.
- **Compare two groups side by side.** Comparison filters let you set one group, such as a region or a tenure band, against another.
- **Combine text search with metadata.** Response-contains filters support AND, OR and NOT, so you can search for "refund NOT shipping" within enterprise accounts in the last quarter.
- **Separate sources.** When a dataset holds more than one feedback column, a Data Sources filter lets you look at each one on its own.
- **Search by ID.** A custom text-search filter can be set to look in any column, including customer or ticket IDs.


The practical result: the question "what are high-value customers in onboarding complaining about on support chat this quarter?" is answerable only if value, journey stage, channel and date were attached before the data arrived.


## A worked example


Imagine a software company with three feedback sources: a quarterly NPS survey, support tickets and app store reviews.


The NPS survey carries account ID, date, plan tier and score. Support tickets carry requester email, date, product area and ticket category. App reviews carry only date, star rating and app platform.


Before analysis, the data team does four things. It maps requester emails to account IDs, so tickets can join to the CRM. It adds a channel column to every row. It maps "product area" and "app platform" to one product list. It joins annual contract value onto every row with an account ID, using the value at the response date.


The result is uneven but usable. Survey and ticket feedback can be cut by tier, product and revenue. App reviews can be cut by product and date only. When a theme about login failures rises, the team can see it in all three channels, size it by revenue in two of them, and say plainly that the app review signal has no account context.


For the connection work itself, see[how to integrate multiple feedback sources](https://getthematic.com/insights/integrate-feedback-sources-analytics-platform) . For choosing a tool, see this comparison of[software for unifying feedback channels](https://getthematic.com/insights/best-software-unify-feedback-channels) .


## Common mistakes to avoid


- **Collecting fields nobody uses.** Every field should map to a question someone will ask. Drop the rest.
- **Stamping the import date instead of the feedback date.** Keep the date the customer gave the feedback.
- **Using today's customer value.** Take value, tier and segment as they stood at the time of the response.
- **Letting each channel name products its own way.** Map to one list before analysis.
- **Filling gaps with guesses.** Leave unknown values blank, and report coverage by channel.
- **Dropping the customer ID to simplify an export.** It's the one field that lets you add everything else later.
